passage:
Thursday, late
Vishal stayed till nine again in the plant lab. He's supposed to finish his internship hours at five, and the marks for this project were settled weeks ago. Today I found him counting root hairs on the millet seedlings, talking to himself, grinning when one tray showed more growth. He asked if he could try the salt test on a second variety "just to see". His father wants him to sit the bank exams, and I've been tempted to tell him research is the safer bet. I won't. It isn't my path to choose. I've given him a key to the side door, the spare microscope and Saturday mornings. Let's see where his curiosity takes him.
– Usha

passage:
Dalia had been the senior conservator at the museum in Accra for eleven years, and she knew the difference between an intern who stayed late for a good report and one who stayed late for the work.
Kofi, twenty, was the second kind. His internship was meant to be about cataloguing. But he kept drifting to the old fishing canoe models in the back store. Every evening he sat with a torch and a notebook, drawing how the tiny nets were knotted. When Dalia asked why, he said, "I want to know how my grandfather's people did it. Nobody writes it down."
His uncle wanted him to study accounting. Kofi mentioned it once, flatly.
Dalia didn't tell him to become a conservator either. She gave him a key to the workroom, a magnifying lamp, and the name of an old net-maker in Jamestown who might talk to him. "See where it takes you," she said.

qa.q: What did Dalia give Kofi?
qa.a: A key to the workroom, a magnifying lamp and the name of an old net-maker in Jamestown.

qa.q: What does Kofi's answer about his grandfather's people suggest about why he stays late?
qa.a: It suggests he is driven by his own curiosity and a wish to preserve something that matters to him, not by marks or a good report.

qa.q: Why was Dalia's choice not to push Kofi toward her own career a wise one?
qa.a: It gave him space and tools to follow his interest wherever it leads, instead of swapping his uncle's plan for hers.

qa.q: How might Kofi feel when Dalia says, 'See where it takes you'?
qa.a: Kofi might feel trusted and free, perhaps for the first time, to follow his curiosity without anyone setting his path.

The ITI workshop in Belagavi closed at five, but Manjula, the senior instructor, kept noticing one bench still lit. Devika, nineteen, enrolled in the electrician course, had found three broken sewing machines in the store and was taking one apart, oil on her wrists, humming.
It was not in the syllabus. There were no marks for it. "Just want to see why the bobbin jams," Devika said, not looking up.
Manjula watched her for a week. Devika stayed late every day, and her notebook filled with drawings of gears.
When Devika's uncle visited and said she should drop all this and prepare for the bank exam, Manjula said nothing against him. She simply cleared a corner bench, labelled it with Devika's name, put a repair manual and a set of small screwdrivers on it, and said, "Use it when you want. Whatever you decide."

qa.a: One of three broken sewing machines from the store.

qa.q: What does Devika's humming and staying late suggest she feels about the work?
qa.a: It suggests she finds real joy and curiosity in fixing the machines for their own sake, since there are no marks for it.

qa.q: Which of Manjula's choices supported Devika best, and why?
qa.a: Clearing a bench with her name, a manual and screwdrivers gave Devika tools and space, while 'Whatever you decide' left the career choice to her.

qa.q: How might Devika's uncle see her late evenings at the workshop?
qa.a: He may see them as a distraction from the bank exam, not realising how much the work lights her up.

passage:
Dear Vandana,
I've been meaning to write this since the end of term.
You probably don't know I noticed, but I did. Every Tuesday and Thursday, after the lab closed, you stayed on with the microscope, looking at pond water. Not for marks. The project was already submitted. I once found you drawing a rotifer at 7 pm with the lights half off, completely lit up.
I've supervised this lab for twelve years. I can tell the difference between a student chasing grades and a student chasing a question.
So here is my offer: the old microscope in the store room is yours to borrow for the summer. And my key to the lab on Saturdays.
You don't need to become anything in particular. Just keep looking.
Francis Sir

qa.a: Francis Sir felt pleased and moved, seeing a student truly lit up by her own curiosity.

So on this teachers' podcast you asked me for a student who surprised me. I'm Mehak, I teach theatre at a college in Pune, and I'll tell you about Leela.
She came to my class because it was an easy credit. Sat at the back, first two weeks, bored.
Then we started building the set for the spring play. And Leela changed. She measured everything twice. She stayed back after rehearsal, painting a brick wall, making it look older with a sponge. At 9 pm, I found her on a ladder, adjusting a lamp to make "evening light".
Her parents want her to do an MBA. I didn't argue with them. That's not my place. I just gave her the keys to the workshop, some old lighting books, and my phone number.
She lit the whole final show. You should have seen her face.

I'm Usha, and I run the conservation room at the city library. I want to write down something I noticed about Manjula, our student volunteer.
She came for the certificate, I think, like most do. Two hours a week. But after a month she started staying until closing. Then past it. I'd find her at the back table, bent over a torn Marathi book from 1910, humming, easing the pages apart with a bone folder.
She never asked if it would count for anything.
Once I heard her whisper to the book, "Nearly there." I don't know what she was thinking. But her face looked the way people's faces look when they're exactly where they belong.
Her father wants her to become a chartered accountant. I didn't say anything about that. I just gave her a spare apron, my old tools, and a key to the back room.

"Bhavna, you ask why I let the new interns choose their own projects. I learned that from one boy.
I, Chaitanya, was a young man of twenty-two, an engineer, when I first mentored interns at the bus depot workshop. One boy, Iqbal, was supposed to learn engine servicing. But every lunch break I found him drawing little seat designs in a notebook, measuring passengers' knees.
Once, I stayed late and found him there at nine at night, building a seat model from cardboard. He wasn't paid overtime. He wasn't being marked.
I could have told him to stick to engines. Instead I gave him a corner of the workshop and scrap metal. Two years later his seat was in forty buses.
When a young person lights up like that, you stand back and hand them tools."

She wasn't acting. She was on a ladder with a torch, rigging coloured paper over the one light to make it look like sunset. She had stayed after rehearsal every night, though lighting earned no marks.
"Hansa, you know this isn't part of your grade?"

Jagdish had planned to push her toward the lead role; her parents wanted her in debate for her CV. He watched her face as the light turned orange. He climbed down, found some old gels in the storeroom and handed them to her. "Your stage," he said.

passage: I've coached debate at the college in Lucknow for fifteen years. I'm Sharmila, and I've seen plenty of students who want trophies. Parveen was different. She stayed after practice, not to prepare for competitions, but to read old speeches and argue about ideas with me. She'd light up when she found a good argument, even one she disagreed with. Her family wanted her in law. I didn't push her away from that. But I gave her my library card, and asked if she'd like to run a reading circle for juniors. She did, and it grew to twenty students. She's now doing a master's in philosophy. I didn't make that choice for her. I only made sure she had room to follow what lit her up.

Mentor log, college robotics lab, Thursday. Sarika
Ishita stayed till nine again tonight. Nobody asked her to; the project marks were submitted last week. She was rebuilding the gripper arm for the third time, just to see if a softer grip could pick up a tomato without squashing it. When it finally worked she laughed out loud, alone in the lab, then photographed the tomato from four angles.
Her father called me last month asking if she should do an MBA like her cousin. I didn't push either way. Today I gave her a spare key card, the old 3D printer nobody uses, and a login for the lab's parts cupboard. Told her: "Break things. Tell me what you learn."
Plan: check in every two weeks, and otherwise keep out of her way.
